title: Kim Gordon’s Capitalist Realism
summary: Kim Gordon’s songwriting with Sonic Youth sought to create a space of subversion between art and politics. Her solo LPs move away from such a project: not out of resignation, but because of the difficulty in creating such a space in today’s hyperpolitics.

title: This Billionaire Is Calling Taxes Soviet Oppression
summary: Sergey Brin’s family fled Soviet authoritarianism, an experience he’s now invoking to portray a proposed wealth tax as Soviet-style tyranny. Ironically this sort of rhetoric is more likely to bring the US closer to today’s Russia: an unabashed oligarchy.
reason: This is primarily a representational story about political rhetoric and ironic framing — a billionaire deploying a historical alibi — but it stays at the content level without illuminating capture mechanics or routing alternatives.

title: How Socialism in the 21st Century Could Work

title: Wartime Iran’s Political Transformation
summary: The US-Israeli war on Iran has strengthened the power of a section of Iran’s elite that earns money in dollars from the sale of oil and petrochemicals. This has unified the state and its elite around an anti-imperialist project but at the cost of permanent austerity.
reason: The story shows how geopolitical enclosure (sanctions, war) routes economic flows toward a dollarized elite while foreclosing alternatives for the Iranian working class — a concrete capture sequence operating through anti-imperialist alibi.
angle: Use the alibi structure tool: the anti-imperialist project functions as the legitimating alibi for elite dollarized accumulation and permanent austerity imposed on the common.

title: We Need to Understand What Makes Capitalism Special
summary: Capitalism is a distinctive mode of economic organization, one that emerged relatively recently in human history. What distinguishes it, a new history argues, is not a reliance on coercion or colonialism but the way it subjects everyone to market dictates.
reason: This is a representational/content-level piece — a book review rehashing definitional debates about capitalism — that doesn't illuminate a specific capture mechanism in operation or show commune-layer activity.

title: Bolivia’s Social Movements Mobilize Against Privatization
summary: In Bolivia, the unions representing miners and peasants have declared an indefinite strike, seeking the resignation of President Rodrigo Paz. They are protesting a new law that undermines peasant and indigenous land rights.
reason: This is a concrete case of enclosure (land privatization attacking indigenous commons) provoking organized resistance through prefigurative coalition-building between miners and peasants routing outside state channels.
angle: Apply the 'commune layer' and 'routing architecture' tools: the strike is not primarily representational — it builds a productive circuit of solidarity between two historically distinct base communities to defend a shared commons against legal enclosure.

title: When Socialists Joined the Rank-and-File Upsurge
summary: Often forgotten today, the US saw a tidal wave of rank-and-file worker militancy in the late 1960s and early ’70s. Many socialists of the era took jobs on the shop floor to help foment the upsurge and build a revolutionary movement to replace capitalism.
reason: This item shows a concrete historical example of routing-level organizing — building alternative productive circuits through shop-floor insertion rather than representational politics — directly relevant to the commune layer and prefigurative institution-building tools.
angle: Use the routing architecture tool to contrast the rank-and-file strategy (changing who routes labor power and through what organizational forms) with the representational trap of electoral socialism, and ask what was actually built versus what was captured.
